summary: This House resolution supports designating November 19, 2025, as National GIS Day and urges GIS users, educators, and innovators to apply the technology for exploration, addressing societal challenges, and economic growth.

scores.thoughts: The resolution recognizes GIS use by Federal agencies but proposes no new programs, funding, or spending changes. It is purely symbolic support for a designated day.
No provisions or references to taxes, tax policy, or revenue measures appear in the bill text.
The bill contains no language related to healthcare systems, coverage, or delivery models.
No connection to firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues exists in the resolution.
The text does not address immigration policy, border security, or pathways to citizenship.
No references to reproductive rights, abortion access, or related regulations are present.
While GIS technology has defense applications, the resolution makes no statements about military spending levels or defense priorities.
GIS is noted as useful for addressing societal issues, but the bill does not advocate for or against environmental regulations or climate policy.
No provisions concerning welfare programs, food assistance, or social safety-net policies are included.
The resolution acknowledges GIS use in STEM classrooms and encourages continued educational application, yet it does not address school funding, federal involvement, or school choice.
The bill has no bearing on drug enforcement, decriminalization, or related criminal statutes.
No language addresses policing, sentencing, rehabilitation, or criminal justice reform.
The resolution does not discuss tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
No fiscal policy, deficit, or debt-reduction measures are mentioned.
The text contains no provisions related to LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
No references to foreign assistance programs or international aid appear.
The bill does not address voting access, election integrity, or electoral procedures.
GIS data sharing is mentioned, but the resolution offers no regulatory stance on data privacy or technology oversight.
No provisions concerning worker protections, union rights, or employer flexibility are present.
The resolution does not engage with religious exemptions or civil-rights protections.
